articles.text: A group of seven Piedmont residents have filed a lawsuit against the City of Piedmont over the dedication and restriping of the Linda Beach tennis courts as full-time pickleball courts. An attorney representing the group, Richard Drury, said that the city has unlawfully violated the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) and that the plaintiffs are seeking an injunction to stop work on the courts as fulltime pickleball courts. “Their position is that the city has approved a project that’s going to have very significant noise impacts on nearby residents,” said Drury. He claimed that at the very least the city had a duty to conduct CEQA review before approving the project. Under CEQA, when a public agency like the city undertakes a project, it must also review the project’s impacts, disclose them to the public, impose all feasible mitigation measures, and analyze all feasible alternative locations, as well as select the environmentally superior alternative location for the project. “Instead, the city did what’s called a CEQA exemption, which means they exempted it entirely from any and all CEQA reviews,” Drury explained. “They didn’t do any environmental analysis[...] even though several experts, including the city’s own expert, suggested that there were a bunch of mitigation measures that the city should consider, like noise barriers or possibly putting [the courts] inside a noise enclosure.” Drury said his clients are currently seeking an injunction to stop the development of the Linda Beach courts until the city conducts a proper CEQA review of the project. It was nearly dark when Program Director Eris Turner raised the scout sign before a crowd of energetic, laughing Cub Scouts near Piedmont Community Hall. Recognizing the universal scouting gesture signaling that it’s time to listen to the adult leader, the scouts settled into their seats next to their parents. From there, Turner separated the fledgling Scouts into groups and sent them off to their respective stations, where they would make arts and crafts, eat snacks, and build boats in preparation for the annual Raingutter Regatta. Twilight Camp is an event for Cub Scouts in the Piedmont Council where they enjoy three evenings of fun activities. Held from Tuesday through Thursday evening, October 24-26, the camp is an introduction to scouting for kids who are thinking about joining. “It’s all about engaging them at this age,” said Turner, a lifelong Piedmont native and veteran Scout. articles.text: After months of deliberation, the City of Piedmont has taken the next step toward creating a memorial of Sidney and Irene Dearing, Piedmont’s first black residents. The city council voted to hire the prestigious design firm, Hood Design Studios in Oakland. The memorial would be located in the triangle park at the intersection of Magnolia and Wildwood Avenues, near the house where the Dearings lived in the 1920s. The Sidney and Irene Dearing memorial is the city’s response to a dark chapter in Piedmont’s history. The Dearings purchased a house in the city in 1924 but were later driven out of the city by a mob of white Piedmont residents. The Piedmont Police Department did little to help at the time, faced with a mob of an estimated 500 people. In the same year the City Council offered to purchase the home from the Dearing family but offered less than the original price. The city wanted to purchase the property to build a street connecting Wildwood and Fairview Avenues. Eventually, the Dearings succumbed to the offer and moved away. The road was never constructed. Discussions about creating a memorial began in May 2022, when City Council considered naming the triangle as “Dearing Family Memorial Park.” The city adopted a resolution directing the Park Commission to explore opportunities to memorialize the Dearing family. Hood Design Studio caught the City’s attention for their extensive body of work on landscape projects reflecting the African American experience. Over the summer of 2023, the City reached out to Hood Design Studio about potential involvement in the project. In August, members of Hood Design Studio met with city staff at Triangle Park to discuss the project and an agreement was reached to move forward with the project. City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore handled the contract Photo by Dearing Family. Sidney and Irene Dearing were the first black homeowners in Piedmont in 1924. and is the City’s primary point of contact with Hood Design Studio. Hood Design Studio is an award-winning social art and design practice located in Oakland, CA, helmed by Creative Director Walter Hood, who readers may recognize as the current Chair of UC Berkeley’s Department of Landscape Architecture & Environmental Planning. Among other things accolades, Hood is a recipient of the 2017 Academy of Arts and Letters Architecture Award, 2019 Knight Public Spaces Fellowship, 2019 MacArthur Fellowship (the “Genius Grant”), 2019 Dorothy and Lillian Gish Prize, and the 2021 recipient of the Architectural League’s President’s Medal award. Hood Design Studio will develop conceptual designs for the memorial. Their team has been in close contact with the city and with the Dearing family to ensure the memorial respects the wishes of the Dearing family. Walter Hood, principal of the firm, is hosting a project kick-off event on Tuesday, November 7 at 5:30 p.m. in the Alan Harvey Theater, 800 Magnolia Avenue. At the event, the designer will discuss his approach to design as a cultural practice, weaving together history, landscape, and memory to express stories through the built environment. Members of the public are encouraged to attend. “If you’re bored in retirement, you could go back to your youth and think about algebra.”

articles.text: On September 24 Troop 11 recognized Arun Brahma’s advancement to Eagle Scout. the highest rank that Scouting offers. He is the Troop’s 137th Eagle Scout. It is a task started by many but accomplished by few. All Eagles have earned the ranks of Scout, Tenderfoot, Second Class, First Class, Star, Life to becoming an Eagle. Each has gone on numerous campouts and adventures, earned at least 21 merit badges, served in troop leadership roles for 16 months or more, and planned and executed an Eagle Service Project. Each Eagle has completed approximately 325 different requirements. On the journey to Eagle, Arun also earned a Gold and Bronze Palm for completing 11 merit badges beyond the required number. For his Eagle Service Project, Arun assembled 40 Welcome Kits for Afghan Refugees in the Bay Area. In 2021, the U.S. abruptly pulled its military forces out of Afghanistan, leaving behind thousands of Afghan residents who had supported the US-backed Afghan government and collaborated with American troops as translators, guides, and contract suppliers, as well as religious and political dissidents. A small number of these Afghani refugees resettled in the Bay Area, which already had a vibrant Afghan community. They are currently rebuilding their lives as they wait for asylum. As a grandchild of immigrants, Arun understood that even under more normal circumstances, coming to a new country is a daunting challenge that takes immense courage. Arun’s project helped these families settle in their new home. Troop 11’s newest Eagle Scout, Arun Brahma. Arun spent several months collecting supplies by reaching out to the local community and businesses for donations. With the assistance of Troop 11 Scouts and leadership, he was able to fill 40 baskets with household items to help Afghani families with basic day-to-day needs. Arun worked with The Afghan Coalition in Fremont to identify the most useful items to include in the kits. The Afghan Coalition is a non-profit community organization that helps Afghan refugees thrive as newcomers. The kits were delivered on April 30, 2023. “This project was especially meaningful to me,” said Arun. “I believe it is very important for minority groups to support each other and especially for US citizens to honor those who have given service to our country, particularly when it is not their own. I hope that these kits will help these families get settled and feel less burdened as they acclimate in their new communities.”

articles.text: With Thanksgiving just around the corner many of us are beginning to fill our dreams with visions of turkey, stuffing, pumpkin pie, mashed potatoes, gravy, and cranberry sauce. For parents of picky eaters, however, those dreams can quickly turn into nightmares. Although the holidays are typically filled with joy, delicious meals, and quality time with loved ones, this time of year can also be a particularly challenging time for picky eaters (and their parents.) What are you supposed to do if your child refuses to eat any of your family’s traditional dishes? What if your child refuses to sit at the holiday table? Here are some tips for surviving the holidays with a picky eater. Maintain a schedule We all know how difficult it is to maintain a consistent routine during the holidays. With that being said, maintaining regular mealtime routines is essential for picky eaters. Children are conditioned to eat certain amounts of food, at specific times of day. Maintenance of this schedule will keep their appetite steady and stable. by reviewing the expectations. Explaining the event, what foods will be there, and your expectations around mealtime behavior (how much to eat, manners) will help your child accept these changes and expectations. Feed your picky eater before the main meal High levels of excitement, adult pressure, and changes in routine are known to suppress appetite. A picky eater who is not necessarily hungry will have a hard time sitting down to eat several unfamiliar foods (many of which are only served during holidays) with large groups of people. In order to make your holiday meal run as smoothly as possible, and keep your child from getting “hangry,” feed your picky eater their preferred meal separately first. Additionally, making sure you include something on the holiday table that they will comfortably eat will make it more likely that they will sit at the table and engage socially with the larger group. Paige Bailey is a pediatric speech language pathologist and feeding therapist, and owner of Speech By The Bay (https://www. speechbythebay.org). Limit things that might be overstimulating Between background conversations, the parade/ game on TV, Aunt Betty’s perfume, and cousins running around the house, the holidays are typically quite overstimulating. Paired with the general increased level of excitement, this stimulation can be extremely disorganizing to a child’s nervous system, which may negatively affect their appetite. Providing quiet spaces and sensory breaks will help limit disruptions to your child’s appetite and eating/sleeping schedule. Preview expectations When you are going to change a child’s typical routine, it is beneficial to prepare them in advance

articles.text: Piedmont High School’s Advanced Acting class presented four rousing performances of The One-Act Play That Goes Wrong from October 19-21 in the Alan Harvey Theater. The student actors, directed by Kimberly Taylor, proudly showcased a production which had been in the works since the second day of school. As this reporter sat in the audience on Friday night, things began to “go wrong.” Three stage hands gathered around the set’s mantlepiece as it barely hung to its place on the wall. With a thud, the audience quieted for a moment, as the sound technician of the play, performed by PHS junior Sophie Hess, buried her face in her hands. In the midst of the chaos creative director Chris Bean, played by Jake Hanke, made his way to audience members with an additional playbill titled The Murder at Haversham Manor, while apologizing for the mistaken The One-Act Play That Goes Wrong playbill. The award-winning play by Henry Lewis, Jonathan Sayer, and Henry Shields is a play-within-a-play. In The One-Act Play That Goes Wrong, the cast is the Polytechnic Drama Society whose members are trying to produce The Murder at Haversham Manor: however, the low-budget production is constantly disrupted by poor actors, mishaps, and set difficulties. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. articles.text: Linnane leads with 6 goals against Castro Valley Piedmont’s boys’ water polo team finished third in the Western Alameda County Conference Championship Tournament after defeating Castro Valley 15-8 on Saturday, October 28 at Encinal, but losing two days earlier in a heated 10-9 overtime match with Berkeley. “Winning league is nice, but our goal is to win NCS (North Coast Section). That’s still in front of us. We played really tough and knew our league had some quality opponents this year. We’re going into NCS feeling confident, I want to see how we respond,” said first year head coach Rik Krumins. The loss to Berkeley finished with controversy. Finn Burke drew a foul a few feet in front of net with four seconds left. However, the scorer’s desk never stopped the clock when the foul was committed and the referees did not have their eyes on the clock. Before Piedmont could set up for a final play time on the clock had expired. Head coach Rik Krumins and assistant coach John Savage instantly made their way to the scorer’s desk to voice their grievance, but to no avail. “They (the officials) have a really tough job and this was a great game. with two really evenly matched teams,” said Krumins. Piedmont’s defeat means their run of three consecutive league titles is over. The goal for a Division 2 North Coast Section championship is still in front of them. PHS enters the NCS postseason with the No. 4 seed and a firstround bye. 15-8 over Castro Valley Piedmont ended the first quarter with a 3-2 lead before getting out to a 9-5 advantage by halftime. Castro Valley drew closer 11-7 in the third quarter, but Piedmont added four goals and conGoalie Luke McAuliffe stretches to stop a shot by Berkeley. Leo Hurwitz scored two goals and had two assists against Berkeley. Staff Photos Piedmont finishes third in the WACC Tournament and looks ahead to the NCS postseason as the No. 4 seed. ceded just one in the fourth. After trailing 1-0, there were back-and-forth possessions before Piedmont’s first score by Declan Linnane with a man-advantage at the 2:50 mark. Peter Krumins then scored two straight goals to go up 3-1 with 1:33 left, while CV scored on its next possession. In the second period, Linnane scored four straight goals to put PHS up 7-2 before conceding the Trojans’ next goal. Linnane added one more to make it 8-3 with 1:23 to go, while George Stein scored at the very last second to make it 9-5 going into halftime. Burke scored 20 seconds into the third, 10-5, but CV scored two to draw closer 10-7 with 2:43 on the clock. Leo Hurwitz scored for Piedmont to make it 11-7 with 37 seconds left in the third. But PHS opened the fourth quarter with three straight goals by Burke, Elles Kreickhaus, and Stein to lead 14-7 with 4:17 to go. CV scored its last goal with 38 seconds left, while Elles Kreickhaus put the exclamation point on the game by scoring with nine seconds left. Final stats: Linnane scored six goals, two assists, and steals. Stein scored two goals, two assists, one steal. Burke scored three goals, one steal. Kreickhaus had two goals and two steals. Krumins scored twice and had one assist. Luke McAuliffe had four saves, Gus von Metszch had two saves and three steals. 10-9 overtime loss to Berkeley The semifinal first quarter ended in a 1-1 deadlock after Burke scored the game’s initial goal 45 seconds in. Piedmont got out to a 3-1 lead in the second quarter with goals from Burke and Hurwitz, but the Yellowjackets eventually battled back to tie 3-3 with 3:27 left in the first half. McAuliffe had a big save with 1:05 left to keep it tied, while Hurwitz had a shot trail narrowly high with 48 seconds. In the first quarter, Reardon tied the match at 1-1 at 5:25, while Melian tied the match at 2-2 at 3:41. This ride is open to all female identifying and non-binary teens. Ride with 6th through 12th grade kids and the amazing coaches. Sign up on www.piedmontdevo.com. On Thursday, October 26, they defeated Lick-Wilmerding 19-13 in San Francisco, but lost 17-7 to Berkeley at the Encinal pool on Saturday, October 28 to pace sixth. The team finished with a 4-16 record. Among Piedmont’s graduating seniors is leading scorer Kat Melian, whose nine goals in a 15-14 win over Lick-Wilmerding marked the team’s best performance since Annika Disney in 2017. 21-5 to Alameda Alameda got out to a quick 6-2 lead by the end of the first quarter and 14-2 by halftime. PHS added two goals in the third, 16-4, while Alameda added five more goals in the final going to finish 21-5. Final stats: Sydney Olson scored twice, while Anne Reardon, Melian and Sophia Nicoll scored individual goals. 19-13 win vs. Lick-Wilmerding The two sides traded goals in the first quarter to a 4-4 deadlock, while Piedmont took a onegoal 7-6 advantage into halftime. Piedmont continued its one-goal lead, 11-10 into the fourth, while the Highlanders put up eight goals in the final going to win it, 19-13. In the first quarter, Reardon tied the match at 1-1 at 5:25, while Melian tied the match at 2-2 at 3:41. Sydney Olson also tied at 3-3 at the 2:17 mark, while Melian put PHS ahead 4-3 with 42 seconds left. Lick-Wilmerding, however, tied it at 4-4 with last-second goal. Lick got out to a 7-4 lead with 3:16 left in the second quarter, but Reardon scored after a minute before Melian scored with a player advantage with 20 seconds before halftime, making it 7-6. Lick-Wilmerding extended the lead to 8-6 after 45 seconds into the third, but the comeback was on from there. Melian added a goal with 6:05 left, while Reardon tied the match 8-8 at the 3:52 mark. After a Lick goal, 9-8, Melian tied the game again at 9-9 with 2:25 on the clock before Reardon put Piedmont ahead after the defense forced a turnover leading to a score with 1:59 on the clock. Then Olson scored to make it 11-9 with 1:27 left. Lick-Wilmerding got one back on their following possession. In the high-scoring fourth, Reardon scored after two minutes, but Lick made it 11-10 on its next possession. Audrey Lam Brown University, Soccer Audrey Lam was named the Post’s Honorable Mention Athlete of the Year in 2023 after helping lead Piedmont High’s soccer team to a 13-1-6 record and winning its first North Coast Section championship in 20 years. She was named the League Player of the Year and won back-to-back firstteam All-League honors in 2023 and 2022. She joined Brown University’s soccer team and won a starting role upon her arrival. She helped the team post a 11-2-1 record and achieve a national ranking of No. 11. Brown will enter the NCAA Tournament starting on November 10. Brown recently won its fourth consecutive Ivy League title and will host the 2023 Ivy Tournament on November 3 against Columbia. This fall she appeared in 14 games, started in 11, and had two goals and an assist. Lam is perhaps the most decorated soccer prospect in PHS history as a three-time invitee to the United States’ Youth National Team. They are introducing biking skills and good trail etiquette to new riders with Fun Rides. The co-ed Piedmont Mountain Bike Team is currently recruiting new riders. The team has fun riding the fantastic local trails and races in the Spring against other East Bay high school teams in the Norcal League (www.norcalmtb.org). Their motto is “Have fun, stay safe” and their season runs from December 1 to the end of May. The team is open to all abilities from beginner to advanced. No experience is necessary. Loaner bikes are available. The Piedmont Mountain Bike Team is partnering with Piedmont DEVO and Oakland DEVO with a GRiT (Girls Riding Together) Ride on December 2nd from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. at Elephant Barn in Joaquin Miller Park. This ride is open to all female identifying and non-binary teens. Ride with 6th through 12th grade kids and the amazing coaches. Sign up on www.piedmontdevo.com. Fun Rides are planned for November 5 and November 12. These rides are open to anyone, and there are no registration requirements until the season starts on Dec 1. articles.text: The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s (SF MOMA) retrospective of Filipina artist Pacita Abad is on view now through January 28. Born in 1946 and from Basco, Philippines, Abad enjoyed a 32-year artistic career and created a vast number of artworks that traverse a diversity of subjects, from colorful masks to underwater scenes to abstract compositions. The artist died in Singapore in 2004, but her colorful artwork uses a variety of mediums and reveals visual, material, and conceptual concerns that still resonate today. “When curator Nancy Lim and I learned that this exhibition was being planned, we knew that it had to come to San Francisco, the city that inspired Pacita Abad to commit her life to artistic expression,” said Eungie Joo, curator and head of contemporary art at SFMOMA. “While some of the works gathered here were shown locally during Abad’s lifetime, this is the first exhibition to reveal the profundity of her prolific practice.” The SF MOMA exhibition features more than 40 pieces, including Abad’s signature trapunto paintings, which are stuffed, quilted canvases adorned with other raw, found materials. Visit https://www.sfmoma.org/ exhibition/pacita-abad/ for tickets and to learn more. Pacita Abad exhibit at SF MOMA

articles.text: The Ruth Bancroft Garden in Walnut Creek is hosting a wreath-making workshop on November 11, just in time for the holidays. True to the nature of Ruth Bancroft’s fauna and foliage, the wreaths will be created using drought-resistant succulents, a signature plant in the garden. An added benefit of succulent wreaths is that they are long-lasting and will be intact long after the holidays. Jennifer Ahlstrand will help guests create these modern takes on the classic ornament. Most of the succulents in the class are locally grown in Ahlstrand’s nursery, WestWind Succulents. Her love of succulent propagation melded into her fine art background. A Walnut Creek native, she has been a frequent guest of the Ruth Bancroft Gardens since the 1990’s. To reserve your spot, visit https://www.ruthbancroftgarden. org /event /workshop -succulent-wreaths/. Succulent wreaths are a modern twist on a holiday classic. articles.text: Byrd, Bull and Bach – Tonality and Color, a solo concert featuring the award-winning harpsichordist Liilian Gordis, will be held this Saturday, November 4 at 5 p.m. at St. Alban’s Episcopal Church. 1501 Washington Avenue in Albany. Born in into a family of scholars and mathematicians in Berkeley, Gordis fell in love with the harpsichord at age 9 and never looked back. Five years later, Pierre Hantaï discovered her during a tour to the United States. He encouraged her to move to France for further studies, and at age 16 she moved to Paris where she was mentored by Hantaï and Bertrand Cuiller. Lillian regularly performs as a soloist in festivals across Europe and the U.S. and plays frequently in a duo with Jérôme Hantaï. Her most recent album, a double-disc dedicated to Bach, was awarded a Diapason d’Or and has received praise in the press worldwide Her first solo recording, Zones, was dedicated to the sonatas of Domenico Scarlatti. In the spring this year she debuted at the Maison Française at New York University during a 6-city U.S. tour with J. Hantaï. She also performed with the Los Angeles Chamber Orchestra. Lillian holds dual nationality with the U.S. and France and resides in Paris. This academic year she is serving as Visiting Assistant Professor of Harpsichord at Oberlin Conservatory in Oberlin, Ohio. About MusicSources MusicSources is a non-profit organization devoted to the historically informed performance of music from the Middle Ages through the Romantic Era (1500 to 1850). It serves as a local, national, and international base for professionals and promising students. Founded in 1985 by Laurette Goldberg, it is now led by JungHae Kim as Artistic Director. Tickets may be purchased at MusicSources.org or at the door using Venmo, credit card, or cash.

articles.text: Young People’s Symphony Orchestra under the baton of David Ramadanoff will present its Fall Concert on November 4 at First Church Berkeley. Young People’s Symphony Orchestra, the oldest youth orchestra in California and the first independent youth orchestra in the nation, will present its Fall Concert this Saturday, November 4 at 7:30 p.m. at First Church Berkeley, 2345 Channing Way. The orchestra will perform Roman Carnival Overture by Berlioz (1843), Rhapsody On A Windy Night by Cavaterra (2022), and Tchaikovsky’s Symphony No. 4 in F minor Op. 36 (1877). Tickets are $20 General admission, and free for students who register at (http://data.ypsomusic.org/tickets). Call (510) 849- 9776 for additional information. Founded in Berkeley in 1936, YPSO is celebrating its 87th season and Maestro David Ramadanoff’s 35th season as Music Director and Conductor. The orchestra has 99 young musicians who range in age from 11 to 21, and hail from throughout the greater Bay Area. YPSO will perform four concerts this year, will be a participant in the California Festival: A Celebration of New Music, and perform at the Bay Area Youth Orchestra Festival at Davies Symphony Hall, before embarking on a 9-day tour to Japan in June 2024, which includes three concerts. The Fall Concert is the kickoff for YPSO’s 87th season. About California Festival YPSO is one of 95 organizations participating in the California Festival: A Celebration of New Music, (cafestival.org) presenting some of the most innovative and compelling music from around the world for two weeks, November 3-19, 2023, in venues throughout the state. Announced in January 2023 and conceived by Los Angeles Philharmonic Artistic Director Gustavo Dudamel, San Diego Symphony Music Director Rafael Payare and San Francisco Symphony Music Director Esa-Pekka Salonen, the California Festival invites musical organizations of all kinds to incorporate works written within the past five years into their broader season programs. About YPSO YPSO’s Music Director, David Ramadanoff, has always been thoughtful about selecting music programs that are able to showcase the diversity of talent in the entire orchestra, and he continues this tradition here. YPSO students engage in a wide range of orchestral music works spanning multiple musical eras and with composers from various backgrounds. Starting this season, YPSO will offer free admission to youth 13 and under accompanied by an adult, and high school and college students with valid ID. YPSO asks that all concert goers, including students, to please register on their ticket site, even if some tickets are free, in order to maintain appropriate seating capacity counts. New musicians invited YPSO is still auditioning for limited sections: trumpet, tuba, French horn, bassoon, and oboe. Piedmont students currently in the band and orchestra are encouraged to audition now to join YPSO for the second half of the season. articles.text: Cal Performances presents the Brad Mehldau Trio at Zellerbach Hall on Saturday, November 11. The award-winning jazz trio consists of pianist Mehldau, bassist Larry Grenadier, and drummer Jeff Ballard. Mehldau and his longtime bandmates have been praised for their musical chemistry and wide range of stylistic and emotional terrain. Mehldau is an iconic jazz soloist in his own right. The New Yorker called him “arguably the greatest working jazz pianist,” with the touch of Bill Evans and the range of Keith Jarrett. He is well-known for his jazz renditions of rock music, including hits by the Beatles and Neil Young. He is the winner of a Grammy award for best contemporary instrumental album, and has been nominated for 13 other Grammies in his career of more than three decades. The trio will perform an evening of original compositions as well as reimagined jazz standards on November 11. The performance begins at 8 p.m. Tickets are available at www. calperformances.org, by phone at (510) 642-9988, or in person at the ticket office at Zellerbach Hall on the UC Berkeley campus. articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre’s Bulrusher, a play by Eisa Davis and directed by Nicole Watson, premiered last week and will be performed through December 3. The coming-of-age story follows protagonist and titular character Bulrusher, a multiracial girl found as an infant floating in a basket on the Navarro River in Mendocino County. The 18-yearold Bulrusher is clairvoyant and struggles with feeling like an outsider in the predominately white town of Boonville. The lyrical comedy takes a turn when the teenager meets a young Black woman from Birmingham who helps her uncover her past. The play deals with difficult topics but is grounded in humor and empathy. “Even though there’s a lot of pain and longing we’re left with, there’s also so much hope,” Davis told the Hollywood Reporter. “So that’s something that has sustaining for me in Bulrusher and a big part of why I wrote it – the possibility for love and forgiveness and joy, even amongst all of this pain.” The cast includes Cyndii Johnson, Rob Kellogg, Jamie LaVerdiere, Shyla Lefner, Jordan Tyson and Jeorge Bennett Watson. Bulrusher is directed by Nicole Watson. Post-show discussions with the cast take place on November 10, 16 and 21. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.berkeleyrep.org/ shows/bulrusher/. articles.text: The San Francisco Mandolin Orchestra makes a return engagement with a concert at Piedmont Center for the Arts on Saturday, November 11. The Orchestra’s season theme this year is “Napoli and the Revolution.” “We chose this theme because the 18th century was a time of revolutionary thought.,” explained Achille Bocus, musical director of SFMO. “Across Europe and America enlightened ideas of freedom, order, rationality, and happiness influenced politics, art, and music. articles.text: Ben Affleck and Anna Kendrick in The Accountant If you enjoy pulp-genre entertainment, then don’t hesitate to spend two hours viewing The Accountant. It’s an unusual thriller that has as its central character a high-functioning, autistic numbers guy, Christian Wolff (Ben Affleck). His clients range from farm families to drug cartels, arms dealers and money launderers. His resume also includes skill sets that allow him to work as a forensic accountant and uncook books that have sprung a leak. When it comes to spreadsheets, he is a savant who can examine a corporation’s profit/ loss statement and sort out where the profits have been going. The film has a number of flashbacks to Wolff’s childhood, which explain how he came to be wearing not only a narrow tie, plastic shirt pocket protector, but is also a black belt in karate. In other words, he is a highly unusual character who is profoundly uncomfortable in social settings. The film opens with Wolff at age 10 or 11 being given a puzzle. While his parents are interviewing a psychologist who runs a group home, the boy assembles a 1,000-piece puzzle upside down. He does this in the time it takes his parents to decide that the home is not for their son. That scene becomes a metaphor, and indeed this film is a puzzle: the challenge is to sort out Wolff’s many idiosyncrasies. Flash forward to the present day. Wolff now operates out of a nondescript office called ZZZ Accounting. He lives in a sparsely furnished apartment and keeps a Streamline trailer in a storage locker, filled with weaponry and incredibly valuable paintings. articles.text: The term B-movie has long been used to refer to second-tier films that ran after the main attraction during the 40s and 50s. In fact, to make sure audiences felt like they received sufficient bang for their buck, going to the movies meant watching a newsreel a cartoon and two feature films. The Bs were hurry-up movies with less well-known stars, smaller budgets, and were the equivalent of dime magazines widely popular during the same time known as pulp fiction. The paper between the covers was rough and cheap (pulpy), the subject matter often gritty detective mysteries, or wildly imagined tales of science fiction or melodramatic westerns. This is all to say that instead of calling a film such as Edge of Darkness a B-movie, it might be more accurate to simply call it pulp cinema. That’s not to imply that such films are not entertaining. Indeed, lacking all pretense, with stripped down plot and dialogue, pulpy movies can entertain and then some. Edge of Darkness uses the familiar and satisfying trope of revenge to move the plot along at an intense clip. Boston Detective Mel Gibson and Shawn Roberts in Edge of Darkness

articles.text: Heartier side dishes and salads fill the bill these days. This grain and squash salad sees a few variations at our table. This version was made with staples from the pantry plus a seasonal delicata squash from the farmer’s market. Wild rice is not technically a true rice but is a cousin. It is the seed of a grass native to the upper Midwest in North America. Any hearty grain can be substituted – farro, wheat berries, barley – as well as other fall squashes such as butternut or kabocha. I prefer delicata squash as it cooks quickly, and the skin is edible. Adding a generous handful of pomegranate arils is delicious, bringing both tartness and texture. We enjoy this salad still warm or at room temperature. If prepared in advance, refrigerating allows the flavors to develop more fully. Wild Rice and Delicata Squash Salad Makes about 5 cups INGREDIENTS • 1 cup wild rice, raw • 1 large bay leaf • 1 medium delicata squash, yielding about 10 – 12 ounces of cut wedges • 1/2 cup pomegranate arils, optional • 1/2 cup walnut pieces, toasted • 1/2 cup fresh flat leaf parsley, rough chopped • 1/4 cup fresh shallots, 1/4” diced • 1 orange, for 1 teaspoon of zest + 2 tablespoons of juice • 2 tablespoons olive oil, extra virgin, plus 1 tablespoon for roasting the squash • 1 tablespoon sherry or apple cider vinegar • 1 teaspoon Dijon-style mustard • 1 teaspoon Mexican oregano, dried leaves lightly crushed • 1 teaspoon ancho chile, ground • 1 teaspoon cumin, ground • 1/2 teaspoon coriander, ground • 1/2 teaspoon black pepper, freshly ground Photo by Deborah Quok • 1/4 teaspoon sea salt, or to taste INSTRUCTIONS Prepare the wild rice according to package directions, adding the bay leaf to the water and salt. Combine the dry spices, pepper, and salt in a small bowl. Prepare the delicata squash. Place an oven rack on the lower third position and preheat the oven to 400°F. Cut the squash lengthwise in half and use a spoon to remove the seeds and membrane. Cut lengthwise again into quartered wedges. Slice these wedges crosswise into 1/ 2-inch pieces. Transfer to a small baking sheet and toss with the one tablespoon of olive oil. Sprinkle two teaspoons of the spice mix over the squash. Roast at 400°F for 15-20 minutes until tender and just beginning to brown on the edges. Remove from the oven and set aside as the wild rice cooks. Make the dressing. Finely zest the orange into a large bowl. Then slice the orange in half across the equator and express 2 tablespoons of juice. Add it to the bowl. Add the vinegar, Dijon mustard, 2 teaspoons of the dried spice mix and mix well. Slowly stream in the olive oil, whisking constantly to develop an emulsified dressing. Add the chopped shallots and let them marinate whilst the wild rice cooks and the squash is roasting. When the wild rice is ready (tender, puffed grains), make sure there is no water remaining in the bottom of the pot. If there is any, transfer the rice to a fine sieve to drain any remaining water. Add the hot wild rice to the dressing and stir to distribute the dressing throughout. Add the roasted squash pieces, pomegranate arils, and chopped parsley. Combine well, taste and add any remaining spice mix as desired. Add toasted walnut pieces just before serving to preserve their crunch. For additional information and to search more recipes, see the blog of Piedmont resident Deborah Quok: https://www. piedmontpantry.com/.

articles.text: Photo by Steve Goodall Kendi was born on Thursday, October 19, at the Oakland Zoo. Oakland Zoo is celebrating the newest addition to the giraffe herd and the start of a new generation and family. After a long pregnancy giraffes have a gestation period of 14-16 months, the zoo’s Kijiji gave birth to her first calf, a female named Kendi, on October 19. At birth, Kendi measured 150 pounds and six and a half feet tall. The new mom, Kijiji, exhibited her protective nature by guiding Kendi into the giraffe barn. A separate area has been set up by the keepers in the barn for the calf and mother giraffe to bond peacefully. This grain and squash salad sees a few variations at our table. This version was made with staples from the pantry plus a seasonal delicata squash from the farmer’s market. Wild rice is not technically a true rice but is a cousin. It is the seed of a grass native to the upper Midwest in North America. Any hearty grain can be substituted – farro, wheat berries, barley – as well as other fall squashes such as butternut or kabocha. I prefer delicata squash as it cooks quickly, and the skin is edible. Adding a generous handful of pomegranate arils is delicious, bringing both tartness and texture. We enjoy this salad still warm or at room temperature. If prepared in advance, refrigerating allows the flavors to develop more fully. Wild Rice and Delicata Squash Salad Makes about 5 cups INGREDIENTS • 1 cup wild rice, raw • 1 large bay leaf • 1 medium delicata squash, yielding about 10 – 12 ounces of cut wedges • 1/2 cup pomegranate arils, optional • 1/2 cup walnut pieces, toasted • 1/2 cup fresh flat leaf parsley, rough chopped • 1/4 cup fresh shallots, 1/4” diced • 1 orange, for 1 teaspoon of zest + 2 tablespoons of juice • 2 tablespoons olive oil, extra virgin, plus 1 tablespoon for roasting the squash • 1 tablespoon sherry or apple cider vinegar • 1 teaspoon Dijon-style mustard • 1 teaspoon Mexican oregano, dried leaves lightly crushed • 1 teaspoon ancho chile, ground • 1 teaspoon cumin, ground • 1/2 teaspoon coriander, ground • 1/2 teaspoon black pepper, freshly ground Photo by Deborah Quok • 1/4 teaspoon sea salt, or to taste INSTRUCTIONS Prepare the wild rice according to package directions, adding the bay leaf to the water and salt. Combine the dry spices, pepper, and salt in a small bowl. Prepare the delicata squash. Place an oven rack on the lower third position and preheat the oven to 400°F. Cut the squash lengthwise in half and use a spoon to remove the seeds and membrane. Cut lengthwise again into quartered wedges. Slice these wedges crosswise into 1/ 2-inch pieces. Transfer to a small baking sheet and toss with the one tablespoon of olive oil. Sprinkle two teaspoons of the spice mix over the squash. Roast at 400°F for 15-20 minutes until tender and just beginning to brown on the edges. Remove from the oven and set aside as the wild rice cooks. Make the dressing. Finely zest the orange into a large bowl. Then slice the orange in half across the equator and express 2 tablespoons of juice. Add it to the bowl. Add the vinegar, Dijon mustard, 2 teaspoons of the dried spice mix and mix well. Slowly stream in the olive oil, whisking constantly to develop an emulsified dressing. Add the chopped shallots and let them marinate whilst the wild rice cooks and the squash is roasting. When the wild rice is ready (tender, puffed grains), make sure there is no water remaining in the bottom of the pot. If there is any, transfer the rice to a fine sieve to drain any remaining water. Add the hot wild rice to the dressing and stir to distribute the dressing throughout. Add the roasted squash pieces, pomegranate arils, and chopped parsley. Combine well, taste and add any remaining spice mix as desired. Add toasted walnut pieces just before serving to preserve their crunch. articles.text: Fred Karren, a longtime Piedmont resident, passed away peacefully in his sleep on October 4, 2023. He was 86. Fred possessed an unparalleled capacity to be interested in people and for friendship. He cared deeply for people, and he positively affected countless lives and organizations. His interests were wide ranging, particularly travel, and the visual and performing arts. He will be greatly missed by his family and his countless friends. Born Fred Lewis Karren on October 17, 1936, in San Antonio, Texas, he was the son of Joe and Mildred Karren. When he was two months old, he moved to Oakland with his family and graduated from Oakland High School in 1954. He attended UC Berkeley where he was a member of Zeta Beta Tau Fraternity. He earned a BS in Business in 1958 and a BS in Architecture in 1968. In 1963, he was introduced to the love of his life, Beth Davis Karren. They were married in 1964 in Toledo, Ohio, and enjoyed 53 wonderful years of marriage until Beth passed away in 2017. Their daughter, Leslie Karren, the apple of Fred’s eye, was born in 1967. In addition to a wonderful father-daughter relationship they enjoyed working side by side in the family real estate business. Fred, Beth, and Leslie, enjoyed many family trips throughout the world, and spending time in their vacation homes in Napa and Palm Desert. He had a career of more than 50 years as an architect. Fred designed or remodeled many homes and retail stores throughout the Bay Area. He served on the Piedmont Planning CommisArchitect Fred Karren died at home in Piedmont on October 4. He was 86. sion for many years and chaired it twice. His architectural expertise was called upon when realtors had a home to sell, and they would seek Fred’s advice on how the home could be remodeled to benefit the new owners. Fred kept active until the very end. On his last night, Fred went to the Opera, had a nightcap with his daughter at her home, kissed her goodnight and said, “See you in the morning, and we will go for coffee.” He enjoyed weekly bridge and dominos games with his friends. He was a big supporter of the arts. He had season tickets and supported the San Francisco Symphony, San Francisco Opera, San Francisco Playhouse, Berkeley Repertory Theater, and many other institutions. He loved animals. He adopted his dog Bentley, an adorable terrier-chihuahua mix, in 2018. He encouraged his friends to do the same because so many dogs, especially senior dogs, need a good home. Over the years he was involved with many clubs and organizations. He was a member of The Pacific Union Club, The Family Club, Claremont Country Club, El Dorado Country Club, Marrakesh Country Club and Temple Sinai in Oakland. He served on the boards of Sinai Memorial Chapel, Jewish Community Federation of the East Bay, Oakland Ballet, Oakland Symphony, Goodwill Industries and the 100 Club. In addition to being survived by his daughter, Fred is survived by his sister Ann Karren Gitlis, his brother-in-law Sam Davis and his wife Joanne Cuthbertson, his nieces Sara Gitlis Schneider (Michael Schneider), Hadley Davis Reierson (Lee Reierson), Carrie Davis (Michael Lebovich), step-niece Jennifer Thomas (Michael), step-nephew Alex Cuthbertson (Elizabeth Meriwether), and five grand nephews, two grand nieces, three step-grand nephews, and one step-grandniece. He is also survived by many extended family members and friends. He was a loyal and great family member and friend. A celebration of life will be held at Claremont Country Club, 5295 Broadway Terrace in Oakland at 1:00 pm on Tuesday, November 7. In lieu of flowers, the family requests donations be made to Temple Sinai, 2808 Summit Street, Oakland, CA 94609; San Francisco Playhouse, 450 Post Street, San Francisco CA 94102; or a charity of choice. A private burial was previously held.

It has been stripped of the family name at the family’s request after a robbery in 1988 when a graduate of Skyline High School and a friend broke into the vault, opened two coffins and removed the skulls of two women. The young men reportedly had a “thing for science fiction and monsters and goblins.” Jane had more stories to share with the group. Frank Norris, who wrote the novel The Octopus, was a member of the Phi Gamma Delta fraternity at Cal in the late 19th Century. The fraternity has custody of his grave, where liquor bottles commonly take the place of flowers. Jane Sather made a gift of Sather Gate to UC Berkeley as a memorial to her husband, but marble panels on it had naked women and men, and an inscription “Erected by Jane K Sather 1909.” She had the panels removed. Jane Leroe also took the walkers up to one of the cemetery’s main attractions, “Millionaires’ Row.” This is where the most grand, elaborate crypts stand, housing some of the cemetery’s most wealthy residents. One is Charles Crocker, one of the “Big Four” who helped bankroll the construction of the transcontinental railroad. Crocker built a mansion on Nob Hill, and also a 30-foot-high fence around three sides of the home of a neighbor who wouldn’t sell him his property. articles.text: Like a number of concepts in the planning world, open space seems to lack a consistent definition among the various organizations that deal with it. In my experience, simply stated, it most often refers to open land, generally public, without (or with very few) buildings. Parks constitute the main and obvious category of open space, in fact “parks” and “open space” are often used interchangeably. One of the best parts of walking through Piedmont is to come upon our well used and well-maintained parks. They are clearly an invaluable and essential part of any city. The universal appreciation of open space is of course due to the many benefits. Recreational uses immediately come to mind – from more active uses like sports that require large fields of lawn or paved courts, to more passive uses like hiking and picnics. The 15-acre Piedmont Park is the city’s only “Community Park”. It is an incredibly beautiful and functional amenity, located in the geographical heart of the city and would be a wonderful and appropriate park for even a much larger city. Considered a Neighborhood Park, popular Dracena is the city’s third largest at 7.8 acres. It includes a number of swings and play structures in addition to large grass areas and a dog run. Parks constitute the main and obvious category of open space, in fact “parks” and “open space” are often used interOpen Space changeably. One of the best parts of walking through Piedmont is to come upon our well used and well-maintained parks. They are clearly an invaluable and essential part of any city. The universal appreciation of open space is of course due to the many benefits. Recreational uses immediately come to mind – from more active uses like sports that require large fields of lawn or paved courts, to more passive uses like hiking and picnics. Protecting and enhancing natural resources is another benefit: ecological issues like air quality and animal, bird and insect habitat are inevitable beneficiaries of green open spaces. Open space can provide a wonderful aesthetic amenity for all of us, and even a partial view of a park’s vegetation can improve property values in a neighborhood. Like any successful public space, open spaces also foster community, bringing peoSee Walking Piedmont on page 31 Photos by Will Adams There are a number of public streets in Piedmont that are a pleasure for strolling, with mature street trees, plus beautiful bosques and planting in people’s yards. This is not technically considered “open space”, but it has almost all the qualities of open space (except access to people’s private property). I call this common valuable amenity “borrowed open space”. The 15-acre Piedmont Park is the city’s only “Community Park”. It is an incredibly beautiful and functional amenity, located in the geographical heart of the city and would be a wonderful and appropriate park for even a much larger city. Crocker Park is a delightful place with a large lawn area, mature pine trees and understory beds of rhododendrons, camellias, azaleas, and ferns. Punctuated with a granite sculpture of a mother bear and cubs by the noted sculptor Benny Bufano – the City’s best known public art – it is considered a mini-park (less than 1acre). Considered a Neighborhood Park, popular Dracena is the city’s third largest at 7.8 acres. It includes a number of swings and play structures in addition to large grass areas and a dog run. Here on the climbing wall, Piedmont free soloists work on their technique. The redwood bosque at Wildwood and Magnolia is a beautiful example of open space that has been created in a typically neglected area. It is one of a number of landscaped traffic islands and medians scattered throughout the city that have been put to good use.

articles.text: Tommy Craven (Mel Gibson) and his only child, daughter Emma Craven (Bojana Novakovic), are leaving his home when a shotgun blast kills Emma. Initially Tommy thinks the shot was aimed at him and wonders who from his past (an ex-con seeking his long contemplated revenge) might have tried to kill him. As he looks for the killers (there are two), he begins to discover pieces to the puzzle that are at first perplexing but soon point not to him as the target but to Emma. It turns out that she worked for a major defense contractor, Northmoor, located in Northhampton, and that she was flirting with the idea of becoming a whistleblower. Since this is pulp cinema there has to be pulp dialogue (here spoken with a Boston accent) in which the Chief of Detectives says to Tommy, “These guys are armed and dangerous,” and Tommy says, “What do you think I am?” Note the lack of ambiguity. Or when Tommy looks at a corporation CEO, who he senses is somehow involved in Emma’s death, and says, “You had better decide whether you’re hanging on the cross or banging in the nails.” What that means is a bit unclear, but no matter, the pulp imagery is spot on, sounding hard-edged and threatening, mirroring Tommy Craven’s perwonderfully portrayed by Mila Kumis and James Franco; and more. While many of the scenes evoke a smile or a chuckle, and are farcical, they are never anything more. Strangely, at the end of the film, as the credits roll, there are a string of wonderful outtakes, several where Fey and Carrell are ad-libbing. I’ll call it the spiritual advantage. In our world of extensive development, our ability to interact with a bit of the natural world (the opposite of the built environment I am always referencing) can raise our spirits, give us a chance to slow down and reflect, to experience our connection to nature—just a little of what the naturalist Henry Thoreau wrote about at Walden Pond in the 1800’s. I suspect the activity of simply strolling through or sitting and resting to enjoy trees, lawns, plants and benches is the most common, and important, use of our open space. There are a number of other sites within Piedmont that contribute to the open space total. These include various EBMUD properties, landscaped medians and traffic islands, various wooded hillsides and ravines, part of the Rose Garden, and even part of the Mountain View Cemetery. Schools, with their large green playfields, seem to be burdened with the inconsistent open space definition mentioned earlier. In Piedmont however, the ongoing joint use of City and School District facilities realistically puts them in the open space category. In addition, because of our proximity and easy access to various nearby regional amenities such as Redwood Park, Temescal Recreational Area, or Joaquin Miller Park, these too can be considered as a part of Piedmont’s useable open space. So, we’re trying to schedule that meeting with the city now.” In recent years pickleball has become a hot-button issue for some Piedmont residents. Since 2018, the sport’s popularity has grown and efforts have increased to accommodate the current number of players.
